summary: Outlines several models for policy based routing and reviews the relative benefits of each approach. It encourages discussion to move toward the model that scales best in a large internetwork.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1104 compares three ways to apply rules to network traffic: control which routes are announced, inspect packets as they pass, or allocate network resources by policy. It discusses their benefits and costs and asks for input on which approach scales.

questions: which policy routing model scales best
what are the models of policy based routing
what are the three policy routing models
subtitle: A comparison of three ways to apply usage policies to network traffic and resources.

tldr.problem: Network operators may need to control access to scarce resources, but policy can be applied in several ways with different costs and levels of detail.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1104 compares policy-controlled route announcements, per-packet filtering and forwarding, and dynamic allocation of bandwidth or buffers.
tldr.outcome: This 1989 memo is a discussion paper that invites comments on models that could scale in a large internetwork; it defines no protocol.

today: The batch metadata gives RFC 1104 no recorded status and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its text describes a 1989 discussion paper and requests comments.

sections.title: Three Policy Models
sections.content:
The memo identifies three models: policy-based distribution of routing information, policy-based packet filtering or forwarding, and policy-based allocation of resources such as bandwidth and buffers. They operate at different levels and may be used separately or together.

Policy can make network behavior predictable according to an administrator's decisions. The memo notes that the models and their interactions need to be considered in advance.
sections.plainLanguage: Rules can control which routes routers share, which individual packets they accept, or how much capacity a type of traffic receives. Some networks may combine these methods.

sections.title: Controlling Route Announcements
sections.content:
The first model enforces policy by controlling which network routes are announced. In the NSFNET example, routing peers and advertised network numbers are checked, while a Routing Policy Data Base controls route metrics and outbound announcements.

The memo says this can support engineering of large networks with little effect on packet-forwarding performance, because policy is applied to routing packets. It does not filter individual packets or reach individual users, and its database needs continuing maintenance.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can apply policy by choosing which destination routes they share. This affects route selection, but it does not inspect every packet or identify individual users.

sections.title: Filtering Packets by Policy
sections.content:
The second model checks traffic on a per-packet basis. Policies can apply at the end-system level and may reach individual users. The memo gives an NSFNET protection mechanism that filters packets by IP destination as an example.

This approach gives detailed control, but checking each packet against policy can affect router performance. The memo also warns that maintaining policies for many networks, end systems and users may require a very large database.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can check each packet against rules before forwarding it. This gives detailed control, but the router and its policy database must handle every packet and rule.

sections.title: Allocating Bandwidth and Buffers
sections.content:
The third model changes resource allocation according to current needs and policy. The memo discusses changing circuit bandwidth and using packet queues that give selected traffic priority, such as network-control traffic.

Dynamic allocation may make resources available when needed without changing routing protocols. However, one network's allocation choices can affect traffic in another administrative domain, so the memo says those policies need technical and inter-domain discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: A network can reserve or prioritize capacity for selected traffic. The rules must account for effects on other networks that carry the same traffic.

sections.title: Accounting Is Related but Separate
sections.content:
The memo distinguishes policy from accounting. Policy sets rules for resource access; accounting combines usage history with policy information and may help trigger policy changes.

Detailed accounting can require collecting and retrieving large amounts of information. The memo also describes a lighter approach that monitors traffic patterns and responds to suspected abuse by changing routing policy or blocking hosts or networks, while noting that statistical detection may react slowly.
sections.plainLanguage: Policy decides what traffic may do; accounting records how resources were used. Usage records can inform policy, but collecting detailed records also has costs.
